summary: Return whether a lowercase sentence contains every letter of the alphabet at least once.
mainInsight: Only presence of each of the 26 letters matters, so collect the distinct letters and check there are 26.

approaches.name: Search for each letter
approaches.summary: For each of the 26 letters check whether it occurs in the sentence.

approaches.name: Count array
approaches.summary: Count occurrences in a 26-slot array and check none is zero.
weaknesses: Stores counts that are not needed

approaches.name: Bitmask
approaches.summary: OR a bit per letter and compare with 2^26 - 1.

personalSolution.approach: Count array of 26 letters, then check that no count is zero
personalSolution.notes: Optimal in complexity. You only need presence, so a set or booleans is enough: len(set(sentence)) == 26.

commonMistakes: Checking only the length of the sentence.
Forgetting to compare with 26 distinct letters instead of the length.
Using counts when presence is enough.
edgeCases: Alphabet missing one letter repeated many times.

cards.answer: Record which of the 26 letters have been seen, using a set or a 26-slot table. Clue: The statement asks whether each of the 26 lowercase letters appears at least once, so only presence matters and a set or a 26-entry table of seen letters answers it.

cards.explanation: Presence of each letter of a fixed alphabet is a membership question; a set counts distinct letters directly.

promptVariants: Do you need letter counts for this problem?
What is the minimal information to keep per letter?
cards.answer: No. A pangram only needs each letter to appear at least once, so one bit per letter is enough. A set of seen letters (or a 26-bit mask) stores exactly that; the sentence is a pangram when the set has 26 members.
cards.explanation: Your counts array works, but it stores more information than the question needs.

promptVariants: Why is `len(sentence) >= 26` not a sufficient test?

options: Letters can repeat: 'a' repeated 30 times is long but misses 25 letters
Letters are uppercase and lowercase, so the length is counted twice
A sentence of length 26 may contain spaces that reduce the letter count

cards.answer: Letters can repeat: 'a' repeated 30 times is long but misses 25 letters
cards.explanation: Length counts characters, not distinct letters. The condition is about the number of distinct letters being 26.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Letters are uppercase and lowercase, so: The input contains lowercase letters only.
incorrectOptionExplanations.A sentence of length 26 may contain spac: The input contains only lowercase letters, with no spaces.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Sorting the sentence first is required t: No sorting is needed; a set answers it directly.

promptVariants: Which input can be rejected immediately without reading it, because of its length?
What cheap early exit is always valid?
options: Any sentence that starts with the letter 'a'
Any sentence whose length is not a multiple of 26
cards.explanation: 26 distinct letters need at least 26 characters, so a shorter sentence cannot be a pangram.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Any sentence longer than 26 characters: Longer sentences may be pangrams, with repeats.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Any sentence that starts with the letter: The first letter says nothing about the others.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Any sentence whose length is not a multi: Pangrams can have any length of at least 26.

promptVariants: Your loop increments letters[...]. What would you change to store less information, and what is the benefit?
Is the counting in your solution necessary? What replaces it?
cards.answer: Counting is unnecessary: replace the counts with booleans (letters[i] = True), a set, or a bitmask seen |= 1 << i, and compare with all 26 present. Time and space are unchanged asymptotically, but the code states the intent (presence) and a set solution is one line.
cards.explanation: Match the data structure to the question being asked.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the set-based solution for a sentence of length n?
Derive the running time of canonicalCode.
cards.explanation: Building the set reads each character once with an O(1) average insertion; len and comparison are constant.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(26 * n): That would be the cost of searching for every letter separately; the set needs one pass, and constants are dropped anyway.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(1): The input is read once, so the cost grows with its length.

promptVariants: The set holds at most 26 distinct letters, so the extra space is O(___).
Space of the set of seen letters: O(___).
cards.explanation: The alphabet size is fixed, so the set never grows beyond 26 entries.
